criteria.name: Introduction — Identifies ethical issues and broad links to engineering design; discusses the context of ethical issues in engineering organisations; identifies relevant stakeholders when considering the ethical issues.
criteria.reasoning: Several issues are identified (product safety versus business competitiveness, end-user harm, professional responsibility) and stakeholders are named. Context within engineering organisations is only briefly sketched as a rapidly growing, competitive industry, and stakeholder interests are not developed in the introduction.

evidence.quote: The relevant stakeholders in this scenario include Rachel, Rachel’s company, the chip contract company, the government health department

criteria.name: Balanced Discussion — Discusses objective arguments for and against decisions on the ethical issues; draws a conclusion on how stakeholders should make decisions about the issues.
criteria.reasoning: Arguments for and against are presented with reasonable depth, including the EACE code and the NHS case. Some arguments rest on assertion, such as the Apple competitiveness claim and the speculative long-term consequences. Recommendations address Rachel and the company, but not the health department or other stakeholders in depth.

criteria.name: Compelling Argument that supports conclusion — The report forms a compelling argument that justifies the conclusion; the body follows a logical structure, with linked paragraphs and content ordered to support the argument; arguments demonstrate a systematic understanding of the ethical issues for all stakeholders.
criteria.reasoning: Structure is logical, with discussion, evaluation, conclusion and recommendations in sequence. However, the conclusion to not ship conflicts with recommending acceptance of the contract. The argument also does not set out conditions under which known defects could be shipped, so the conclusion is only partly supported.

Rachel should accept the contract with the government health department.

criteria.name: Research and Evidence — Arguments are substantiated with adequate references and qualitative/quantitative evidence; research demonstrates a balanced, in-depth understanding of the topic.
criteria.reasoning: Four references are cited, including reputable sources (Engineers Australia code, BBC, NYT) and some quantitative reasoning (500 failed servers). Evidence is thin and partly misapplied: the CNBC source is a marketing article, and the Volkswagen case is misdescribed. No academic ethics literature is used.

evidence.quote: This approach meets consumer demand for innovation while outpacing large competitors like Samsung and Google

criteria.name: Report Structure, Format and Language — The report includes appropriate sections serving their functions (abstract, introduction, body, and conclusion); maps, figures, tables, and visual elements are correctly used to support discussion; writing is grammatically correct, fluent, concise, easy to read and understand, and uses appropriate word choice; references are well-structured and appropriate, supporting the report’s motivations.
criteria.reasoning: The report has introduction, discussion, conclusion and recommendations, but no abstract. No figures or tables are used. Several typos and grammatical errors appear, and references have malformed URLs and incomplete entries.

evidence.quote: DICUSSION: To Ship or Not to Ship
a series ofIT system failures in NHS hospitals across England

technical_issues.issue: The Volkswagen case is misdescribed. The defeat devices manipulated emissions tests on diesel vehicles, not crash-safety tests on electric vehicles.
The HSSIB/NHS case concerns IT and records system failures, not hardware defects. Calling it an 'almost identical malfunction scenario' and attributing deaths to it overstates the causal link.
The claim that Apple's release cycle outpaces Samsung and Google is supported only by a marketing-focused CNBC article, which does not substantiate the competitive claim.
The 1 percent failure rate across 5,000 servers is an unstated assumption presented as a basis for harm estimates without justification.

Recommendation 1 (accept the contract) sits uneasily with the conclusion that not shipping is most ethical. The report gives no criteria for when defective products could be shipped, which R2 requires.
Reference [4] has a garbled author list, reference [3] lacks an author and URL, and reference [1] has a malformed URL. The 'EACE' abbreviation is non-standard.
No abstract is included, though the task requires one of approximately 150 words.

overall: A logically structured report with reasonable stakeholder coverage and a clear recommendation. It is weakened by a missing abstract, no visuals, thin and partly misapplied evidence (including a factual error on Volkswagen), an unresolved contradiction in the recommendations, and no shipping criteria. Estimated total 32/50.

feedback.summary: You have written a clearly structured report that identifies the ethical tension between product safety and business competitiveness, and names the main stakeholders. Your discussion and use of evidence give you a solid base. To move up, tighten the link between your conclusion and recommendations, correct the factual points in your case studies, and add the abstract and visual elements the brief asks for.
next_steps: Add an abstract of about 150 words, and include at least one visual, such as a stakeholder map or a decision flowchart, that supports your discussion of whether to ship.

Set out explicit criteria for when known-defect servers could ever be shipped, such as defect severity, disclosure and mitigation, and make Recommendation 1 consistent with your conclusion that not shipping is most ethical.

Correct the Volkswagen case, state the assumptions behind your 1 percent failure-rate estimate, and replace the marketing-focused CNBC source with evidence that supports the competitiveness claim. Then extend your recommendations to the health department and other stakeholders.

criteria.C1: You identify several ethical issues, including product safety against competitiveness, harm to end users and professional responsibility, and you name key stakeholders such as Rachel, her company, the chip contractor and the health department. To reach Excellent, place these issues more fully within the context of engineering organisations, such as quality-assurance pressures and reporting lines, and explain how each stakeholder's interests differ.
criteria.C2: Your arguments for and against shipping have reasonable depth, and you use the engineering code and the NHS case to weigh them. Some claims rest on assertion, such as the Apple competitiveness point and the speculative long-term consequences. Ground each argument in evidence, and give decision guidance to the health department and other stakeholders, not only Rachel and the company.
criteria.C3: Your report follows a logical sequence from discussion to evaluation, conclusion and recommendations. However, your conclusion that not shipping is most ethical is only partly supported, because you recommend accepting the contract and do not give criteria for when known defects could be shipped. Set out those conditions explicitly so that your arguments and recommendations clearly support your conclusion.
criteria.C4: You cite several reputable sources, including the Engineers Australia code, the BBC and the New York Times, and you use some quantitative reasoning, such as the 500 failed servers. Some evidence is weak or misapplied: the CNBC article is marketing-focused, and the Volkswagen case concerns emissions-test manipulation on diesel vehicles. Use sources that directly support each claim, and add academic ethics literature.
criteria.C5: Your report includes the core sections (introduction, discussion, conclusion and recommendations) and is generally readable. It lacks the required abstract and includes no figures or tables to support the discussion. Add an abstract, include at least one visual, proofread carefully for typos and grammar, and make every reference complete with author, date, title and a working link.
